source: Hu, Cheng, Chiu, Paller (2020) Promoting memory consolidation during sleep: a meta-analysis of TMR
finding: First meta-analysis of sleep TMR. Overall effect is small but reliable.
numbers: 91 experiments, 212 effect sizes, N=2004. Overall Hedges g=0.29, 95% CI 0.21-0.38.
limits: Most studies small; multilevel model; see publication bias line.
agent_relevance: Anchor: cueing replay is causal but modest. Expect small gains from any reactivation step in the agent.

source: Hu et al. (2020) meta-analysis: cueing stage moderator
finding: Effect depends on sleep state. Works in NREM, not in REM or wake.
limits: REM has only 7 experiments. Wake cues were mostly not EEG-checked.
agent_relevance: Reactivation helps only in the right state. For the agent: a replay pass needs a quiet state with no new input.

source: Hu et al. (2020) meta-analysis: learning type moderator
finding: TMR helps declarative and skill memory but not conditioning (fear).
limits: Conditioning has 4 experiments, 91 people; wide CI, not proof of no effect.
agent_relevance: Fear TMR result is null overall; matches the mixed results for fear.

source: Hu et al. (2020) meta-analysis: outcome and design moderators
finding: Recall and performance measures show the effect; recognition, skin conductance and subjective ratings do not.
numbers: Recall g=0.24; performance g=0.40; recognition g=0.18 [-0.04,0.40]; SCR g=-0.08; subjective rating g=0.11. Within-subject g=0.25 vs between-subject g=0.28 (Q=0.055, p=.81).
limits: Outcome categories overlap with task types.
agent_relevance: Cueing sharpens measurable performance, not felt confidence. Do not use self-rated confidence to judge a replay pass.

source: Hu et al. (2020) meta-analysis: cue modality moderator
finding: Sound and odor cues work about equally well.
numbers: Auditory verbal g=0.26 (k=74); auditory nonverbal g=0.23 (k=94); olfactory g=0.32 (k=32). Q(2)=0.69, p=.709.
limits: Modality is confounded with task and lab.
agent_relevance: The cue content matters less than its link to the encoded memory. Any consistent tag could serve as an agent cue.

source: Hu et al. (2020) meta-analysis: publication bias analyses
finding: Published effects are larger than unpublished. Corrected estimates are about half the headline.
numbers: Published g=0.31 [0.22,0.41] (k=186); unpublished g=0.18 [-0.06,0.42] (k=26). Three-parameter selection model g=0.13 [0.06,0.21]. A-priori selection models g=0.21, 0.17, 0.15; severe one-tailed g=-0.05.
limits: Severe one-tailed bias scenario removes the effect.
agent_relevance: Treat 0.29 as an upper bound; true effect maybe 0.13-0.2. Be cautious about big claimed wins from replay.

source: Rasch, Buchel, Gais, Born (2007) Odor cues during slow-wave sleep prompt declarative memory consolidation (Science)
finding: Founding study. An odor present during learning, re-presented in SWS, improved retention of card-pair locations (hippocampus-dependent) but not finger tapping (procedural). Ineffective in REM, in wake, or if odor was absent at learning. fMRI showed hippocampal activation to odor in SWS.
numbers: Abstract only read. Effect sizes from meta-analysis rows: Exp1 spatial g=0.69 [0.19,1.18] (N=18); Exp1 finger tapping g=-0.08; Exp3 REM spatial g=-0.05 (N=17); Exp5 SWS g=0.64 [0.05,1.22] (N=12).
quote: reactivation indeed causes memory consolidation during sleep
limits: Small N per experiment; full text not read this session.
agent_relevance: Shows replay is causal, with three boundary conditions: state, memory type, learned context link.

source: Rudoy, Voss, Westerberg, Paller (2009) Strengthening individual memories by reactivating them during sleep (Science)
finding: Sound cues played in NREM improved memory for specific object locations. The effect is item-specific: 25 cued vs 25 uncued objects in the same person.
numbers: N=12 nap. Error cued 1.07 cm (SE 0.08) vs uncued 1.23 cm (SE 0.10), t(11)=2.6, p<.05. Benefit in 10 of 12 people. Participants at chance guessing which sounds were played.
quote: Consolidation thus operates during sleep with high specificity
limits: Awake control (N=12): cued 1.15 vs uncued 1.32 cm, t(11)=1.4, p=.18 (ns). Meta row g=0.48 [-0.08,1.04], ns.
agent_relevance: Replay can be aimed at single items, not just whole sessions. Supports a per-item reactivation operator.

source: Rudoy et al. (2009) EEG sub-result
finding: Brain response to the cue in sleep tracked how much was forgotten.
numbers: Median split on pre-post accuracy: EEG amplitude 600-1000 ms after sound onset was 15.3 microvolts larger when forgetting was less, t(11)=3.2, p<.01. Less-forgetting items 0.51 cm better post-nap; more-forgetting 0.60 cm worse.
limits: Median split; correlational.
agent_relevance: Cue-evoked response predicts benefit, a readout that reactivation took hold. Agent analogue: check a cued item was actually retrieved.

source: Cousins, El-Deredy, Parkes, Hennies, Lewis (2014) Cued memory reactivation during SWS promotes explicit knowledge of a motor sequence (J Neurosci)
finding: Extends TMR to procedural learning: tones from one of two 12-item finger sequences were replayed in SWS. Cued sequence gave more explicit knowledge and faster skill.
numbers: N=32 (16 TMR, 16 control cued before sleep). Explicit knowledge p=0.005; procedural skill p=0.04; fast spindles (13.5-15 Hz) at motor regions predicted skill gain r=0.71, p=0.01. Control group: no cue effect.
limits: Control received cues before sleep, not awake after; small N.
agent_relevance: Reactivation can turn implicit knowledge into explicit. Agent analogue: replay may help articulate a rule it only used.

source: Cousins, El-Deredy, Parkes, Hennies, Lewis (2016) Cued reactivation of motor learning during sleep leads to overnight changes in brain activity (PLoS Biol)
finding: fMRI follow-up: cued sequence faster next day; caudate and hippocampus activity (cued vs uncued) related to SWS time, cerebellar and motor cortex activity to REM time. Caudate-hippocampus connectivity rose.
numbers: Abstract-level findings only; numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract-level extraction.
agent_relevance: Different sleep states may carry different parts of consolidation.

source: Cairney, Durrant, Hulleman, Lewis (2014) TMR during SWS facilitates emotional memory consolidation (Sleep)
finding: Cues in SWS helped emotional (negative) picture-location memory more than neutral, but only in response times and only as a function of SWS and spindles.
numbers: N=15 adults, 72 picture-location pairs (36 negative, 36 neutral), nap. Three-way interaction significant for RT, not accuracy. SWS duration and spindles predicted faster judgments for cued negative vs neutral.
limits: Small N; effect on RT not accuracy; covariate-driven.
agent_relevance: Emotion changes which cued items get consolidated. Salience tags interact with reactivation.

source: Cairney, Lindsay, Sobczak, Paller, Gaskell (2016) Benefits of TMR are contingent on memory accuracy and direct cue-memory associations (Sleep)
finding: TMR helped weakly learned items (low pre-sleep accuracy) but not strongly learned ones. No benefit for items only indirectly linked to the cue (picture-word pairs).
numbers: N=30 nap; 50 pictures each. Overall TMR x time interaction F(1,29)=4.00, p=0.055 (marginal). Low-accuracy items benefited; benefit predicted by SWS time. Picture-word pairs: no benefit. Effect vs number of replays r=0.23, p=.22.
limits: Median split of items; overall effect marginal.
agent_relevance: Replay targets weak memories: prioritise low-confidence items. The cue must point directly at the thing to strengthen.

source: Cairney, Guttesen, El Marj, Staresina (2018) Memory consolidation is linked to spindle-mediated information processing during sleep (Curr Biol)
finding: Verbal cues in a nap evoked fast spindles; memory category (object vs scene) could be decoded in that window and decoding fidelity predicted benefit.
numbers: N=46 (27 nap, 19 wake). Next-day (T3) retention: TMR main effect F(1,44)=4.65, p=0.04; TMR x group F(1,44)=3.94, p=0.05. Nap group cued>uncued t(26)=3.83, p=0.001; wake group t(18)=0.09, p=0.93. Retention at T2 unaffected by cueing (F=0.19, p=0.66). Benefit vs number of cues rho=0.02.
limits: Correlative decoding; benefit only at T3.
agent_relevance: Reactivation carries content, and the benefit appears after a night, not immediately. Delayed read-out of replay gains.

source: Hu, Antony, Creery, Cairney, Paller (2015) Unlearning implicit social biases during sleep (Science)
finding: Counter-stereotype training paired with a sound; replaying the sound in SWS reduced the cued implicit bias more than the uncued one, and the difference lasted one week.
numbers: N=40, with built-in direct replication. Cued/uncued x pre/post F(1,39)=14.61, p<.001, eta2=0.273. Cued bias fell t(39)=2.70, p=.010; uncued unchanged. At 1 week (n=38) F(1,37)=4.67, p=.037. About 258 cue presentations.
limits: Cued vs baseline at 1 week: interaction not significant (F=0.47, p=.50).
agent_relevance: Reactivation can strengthen a correction of a bias, not only a fact. Links to the debiasing subfield.

source: Henin et al. (2019) Closed-loop acoustic stimulation enhances sleep oscillations but not memory performance (eNeuro, negative results)
finding: Failed replication. Closed-loop sound raised slow oscillations and spindles but did not improve memory in a VR navigation task (N=12) or a double-blind word-pair replication (N=19).
numbers: Exp1 N=12 crossover; Exp2 N=19, powered 95% for a moderate effect. No behavioural difference between real and sham stimulation in either.
quote: Enhancement of sleep oscillations may be insufficient to enhance memory
limits: Closed-loop stimulation, not item-specific TMR.
agent_relevance: Strengthening the oscillation is not the same as strengthening memory. Beware proxy metrics that look like progress.

source: Closed-loop TMR at slow-oscillation up vs down states (Sci Rep 2019)
finding: Vocabulary cues at slow-oscillation up-states improved recall; down-state cues did not clearly help. The up vs down behavioural contrast was not robust.
numbers: N=16. Up-state remembered words: theta t15=2.69, P=0.008; spindle t15=2.50, P=0.012. Down-state: theta t15=0.68, P=0.253; no spindle difference. 120 words, 80 cued, 90 min cueing.
limits: First author not checked; no robust behavioural up vs down contrast.
agent_relevance: Timing of replay within the cycle matters at brain level, weakly at behaviour level.

source: Cordi, Diekelmann, Born, Rasch (2014) No effect of odor-induced memory reactivation during REM sleep on declarative memory stability (Front Syst Neurosci)
finding: Odor reactivation in REM did not protect memory from later interference, unlike earlier SWS findings.
numbers: Recall after REM odor 54.16 +/- 5.93% vs vehicle 52.86 +/- 6.49%, p=0.87.
limits: One paradigm (interference after waking); a null.
agent_relevance: Confirms state dependence: replay in the wrong state does nothing.

source: Purple, Sakurai, Sakaguchi (2017) Auditory conditioned stimulus presentation during NREM sleep impairs fear memory in mice (Sci Rep)
finding: Fear: re-presenting the tone in NREM, but not REM, impaired later fear memory in mice. This is the opposite direction to enhancement.
numbers: Trace fear conditioning; NREM-cued mice froze significantly less to the CS; REM-cued and control did not. Context discrimination trends not significant.
limits: Mouse study; effect numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: The sign of reactivation depends on content and state. Reactivating a bad memory can weaken it.

source: Fear synthesis: Hu 2020 human conditioning null versus mouse NREM weakening
finding: Human fear-conditioning TMR pooled to nothing while mouse NREM cueing weakened fear. Results are mixed; sign and size unclear.
numbers: Conditioning g=-0.03, 4 experiments, N=91 humans; SCR outcome g=-0.08 (4 effect sizes).
limits: Different species and paradigms; my synthesis.
agent_relevance: Do not assume replay always strengthens. Replaying a flawed belief may entrench or dilute it.

source: Update on recent advances in TMR during sleep (npj Science of Learning 2024 review)
finding: Recent review: some declarative effects did not replicate; most TMR studies are small; calls for large preregistered multi-lab studies. In one motor study no effect at 24 h but a cued advantage at 10 days that vanished later.
numbers: Rakowska et al. as summarised: no effect at 24 h, better cued sequence at 10 days, gone after another 6-8 weeks.
quote: Several studies have recently failed to find a significant difference
limits: Review; individual numbers not checked.
agent_relevance: Gains from replay can be delayed and temporary.

source: Behrouz, Hashemi, Javanmard, Mirrokni (2026) Language Models Need Sleep (arXiv 2606.03979)
finding: LLM Sleep paradigm: consolidation by distilling a small model into a larger one, then Dreaming (RL-made synthetic rehearsal data). Not cue-based TMR but a sleep-inspired replay for LLMs.
numbers: Knowledge incorporation (SQuAD no-context), single passage: base 31.9, fine-tune no dreaming 33.4, SEAL 46.7, Sleep 48.1, Sleep four-level 48.9. Math Qwen3-8B AIME-24: Sleep 79.2 vs GRPO 76.4, SFT 75.5. Removing Dreaming drops a knowledge ablation to 35.7/36.2.
limits: Authors own benchmarks; no cue targeting; not a TMR test.
agent_relevance: Replay with self-generated rehearsal data beats fine-tuning alone; Dreaming is the biggest ablation effect. Idea for an offline rehearsal operator.

source: Lee, McLeish, Fanti, Goldstein (2026) Do Language Models Need Sleep? Offline Recurrence (arXiv 2605.26099)
finding: Model periodically converts recent context into fast weights through N offline recurrent passes before clearing the KV cache. More sleep passes help most on deeper reasoning.
numbers: Cellular-automata task: no loop about 10% exact accuracy after ~5B tokens; 2 loops ~20%; 3-4 loops above 30%.
limits: Synthetic and math tasks; architecture-specific; no cue targeting.
agent_relevance: Extra offline compute on stored experience improves later answers; supports an offline consolidation state in the schema.

source: Personalized TMR enhances consolidation of challenging memories (arXiv 2511.15013, 2025)
finding: Cue frequency adapted to each person recall and difficulty reduced memory decay for hard items, with stronger slow-wave and spindle coupling.
numbers: Group (personalized, TMR, control) x time, all items: group F(2,66)=5.10, p=0.009; time F(1,66)=42.42, p<.001; interaction F(2,66)=0.74, p=0.479. Difficulty ratings vs accuracy rho=-0.878 to -0.948.
limits: Overall interaction not significant; benefit only in difficult subsets; N=12 per group.
agent_relevance: Allocate replay by difficulty: more cues for items the system finds hard. Matches Cairney 2016.

source: Synthesis: reliability conditions across TMR studies (Hu 2020, Cairney 2016, Henin 2019)
finding: Positive and null results coexist. Better predictors of success are weak initial memory, direct cue link, NREM, verified sleep.
numbers: Meta moderators plus Cairney 2016 and Henin 2019 as above.
limits: My synthesis line, not a new study.
agent_relevance: Write the agent replay step with explicit conditions (weak items, direct cues, quiet state) and measure each.

source: Theory line: active systems consolidation and spontaneous replay underlie TMR (introductions of Hu 2020, Cairney 2018, Cousins 2014)
finding: Theory: new memories are reactivated spontaneously in NREM, coordinated by slow oscillations, spindles and hippocampal ripples, and gradually moved to cortex. Cues bias which memories are replayed.
numbers: Meta-analysis cites a standard two-stage model; Cairney 2018 ties cue-evoked fast spindles to decodable content.
limits: Theory only; no formal model in these papers.
agent_relevance: Agent analogue: short-term store, an offline pass, long-term store, with cues biasing what is replayed.

source: Cross-study: sleep-state physiology predicts TMR gain, cue count does not (Cairney 2018, 2016; Hu 2015; Cousins 2014)
finding: Across studies the benefit correlates with SWS time or spindles, not with cue number.
numbers: Cairney 2018 rho=0.02 with cue number; Cairney 2016 r=0.23 ns; Hu 2015 prediction from SWS x REM minutes; Cousins 2014 spindles r=0.71.
limits: Correlational, small N.
agent_relevance: More replay is not better; the quality of the state matters. Cap replay and check state.
